title: Phetchaburi–Ratchaburi 3-Day Trip: Old Town, Markets & More | ThailandAddict
metaDesc: A two-province road trip through Phetchaburi and Ratchaburi, Thailand: old-town temples and Khao Wang, then Ratchaburi's Tao Hong Tai pottery and Khao Ngu, ending at Damnoen Saduak floating market — with times, prices and a route that never doubles back.
keywords: Phetchaburi Ratchaburi trip, two-province itinerary Thailand, Damnoen Saduak floating market, Tao Hong Tai, Khao Wang, Ratchaburi dragon jars
h1:
Phetchaburi–Ratchaburi in 3 Days
Old Town, Dragon Jars & Floating Market
intro: Phetchaburi and Ratchaburi sit only about 54 km apart — an hour's drive — so it's easy to do both in one go. This trip starts in Phetchaburi's old town, with its handsome temples and famous sweets, climbs Khao Wang for a view over the whole city, then moves north into Ratchaburi for the Tao Hong Tai dragon-jar pottery, Khao Ngu, and the old riverside quarter along the Mae Klong. It wraps up with an early start for a boat ride at Damnoen Saduak floating market. The route flows steadily northward so you never have to backtrack, and it works whether you're driving yourself or taking public transport and renting a car in town.

blocks.html: Plenty of people assume Phetchaburi and Ratchaburi need separate trips, but the two provinces are next-door neighbours, linked by Phetkasem Road (Highway 4). It's about 54 km city centre to city centre — roughly an hour's drive — so they fit neatly into a three-day trip that works its way south to north. Day one covers Phetchaburi's old town and Khao Wang, day two moves up to Ratchaburi for ceramics and nature, and day three starts early at Damnoen Saduak floating market before heading home. That rhythm means no rushing and no driving back on yourself.

blocks.title: Before you set off
blocks.html: If you're driving yourself, there are two routes down to Phetchaburi from Bangkok: Rama 2 Road through Samut Sakhon–Samut Songkhram, or Phetkasem Road through Nakhon Pathom–Ratchaburi — about 2 hours to Phetchaburi town either way. For the Phetchaburi–Ratchaburi leg, take Phetkasem straight north, roughly 1 hour. There are vans and trains running between both cities for those without a car, but for a cross-province trip like this, renting a car or driving yourself is far more flexible, since the sights are spread out beyond the town centres.

blocks.text: Day 1 — Phetchaburi old town, temples and sweets, then up Khao Wang

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Phetchaburi old town → Khao Wang → overnight in Phetchaburi

items.activity: Leave Bangkok, head for Phetchaburi town
items.note: Set off early to beat the traffic; you'll reach Phetchaburi around 10:30, just in time for a late breakfast in the old town.

items.activity: Wat Mahathat Worawihan — white five-spired prang in the city centre
items.note: Phetchaburi's signature temple. Take in the stucco work and murals; free entry, dress modestly, about 40 minutes.

items.activity: Wat Yai Suwannaram — teak sermon hall and carved doors
items.note: A few minutes from Wat Mahathat. Genuine Phetchaburi craftsmanship — don't skip it if you like timber architecture.

items.activity: Lunch in the old town + Phetchaburi sweets
items.note: In the hot season try khao chae; year-round there's mor kaeng custard and thong yip / thong yot, easy to find all over town.

items.activity: Old-building café in the old quarter, an afternoon break from the heat
items.note: Several old-building cafés have opened along the town's streets over the past couple of years — a good place to dodge the sun before the climb.

items.activity: Phra Nakhon Khiri Historical Park (Khao Wang)
items.note: Take the cable car up and back, see the King Rama IV summer palace and views over the city. Late afternoon means softer sun — watch out for the monkeys.

items.activity: Come down the hill, find a place to stay in Phetchaburi town
items.note: Spending the first night in Phetchaburi sets you up to drive north to Ratchaburi the next morning. Keep dinner simple in town.

blocks.html: Khao Wang is the highlight of day one. Entry is a few tens of baht for Thais, around 150 THB for foreigners, plus roughly 50 THB for the cable car up and down. It's open about 08:30–16:30, so if you want to go up, aim to arrive before 4 pm to have time to walk around. You can take the stairs if your legs are up to it, but the cable car is easier. There are lots of monkeys at the top — keep snack bags and water bottles zipped away and don't tease them.

blocks.title: Why stay in Phetchaburi town the first night
blocks.html: Many people like staying in Cha-am on the first night for the beach, but for this trip crossing into Ratchaburi, staying in Phetchaburi town lets you drive straight north the next morning instead of looping back. If you want the beach, save Cha-am for another trip — or tack it on at the end instead.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Drive up to Ratchaburi: Tao Hong Tai, Khao Ngu, the old Mae Klong quarter

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Phetchaburi town → Tao Hong Tai → Khao Ngu → Ratchaburi old town → overnight near Damnoen Saduak

items.activity: Leave Phetchaburi town, drive up to Ratchaburi via Phetkasem Road
items.note: About 54 km city centre to city centre, roughly an hour's drive, passing through Pak Tho district before reaching Ratchaburi town.

items.activity: Tao Hong Tai — ceramics factory and dragon-jar workshop
items.note: On Chedi Hak Road, Mueang district. Free entry, open around 08:00–17:00. Walk through the kilns and pottery, with an in-house workshop and café — Ratchaburi's go-to craft check-in spot.

items.activity: Khao Ngu Stone Park — limestone hills with a lake in the valley
items.note: About 8 km from town, with old Buddha-image caves, a lake and limestone views. Good for a stroll and photos; there are several restaurants with Khao Ngu views nearby.

items.activity: Lunch at a Khao Ngu view restaurant
items.note: The Khao Ngu area has several Thai restaurants with mountain and rice-paddy views — à la carte dishes and seafood at friendly prices.

items.activity: Ratchaburi National Museum + a walk through the old Mae Klong riverside quarter
items.note: The museum sits in the former provincial hall, a building nearly 80 years old, telling Ratchaburi's story from the Dvaravati era onward. From there you can walk on into the old market quarter along the Mae Klong.

items.activity: A Ratchaburi café for an afternoon break
items.note: Ratchaburi has plenty of new farm cafés and riverside cafés — pick one to settle into before moving over towards Damnoen Saduak.

items.activity: Drive over to stay near Damnoen Saduak
items.note: It's about 30 km from Ratchaburi town to Damnoen Saduak. Stay near the floating market so you can be up early for the morning atmosphere the next day.

blocks.html: Ratchaburi is famous for pottery, especially the dragon jars that have been a hallmark of the city for over sixty years. Tao Hong Tai is a long-running factory open to visitors for free, where you'll see both the old kilns and contemporary ceramic work. Khao Ngu, meanwhile, is a limestone hill that was once a quarry and has since been turned into a public park, with old Buddha-image caves and a lake to wander around. Together with the old Mae Klong riverside quarter, those two spots give day two a mix of craft, nature and history all in one day.

blocks.title: Which side to stay on for the second night
blocks.html: If your goal is Damnoen Saduak floating market the next morning, it's worth staying around Damnoen Saduak or near the market, so you can be up in time for the busy early hours before the crowds build. Lodging here ranges from canal-side resorts to homestays, and weekday rates are noticeably cheaper than weekends.

blocks.text: Day 3 — Damnoen Saduak floating market: boat ride, local food, then home

blocks.label: Day 3
blocks.title: Damnoen Saduak floating market → boat ride → souvenirs → back to Bangkok

items.activity: Get into Damnoen Saduak floating market early
items.note: The market gets going from early on, around 07:00 onward. Arrive early for the more traditional feel and fewer crowds — great photos of the paddle boats selling their wares.

items.activity: Boat ride along Khlong Lat Phli
items.note: Hire a paddle boat or long-tail to see the canal-side houses. Agree the rental price before you get on; you can buy food both on the boat and along the bank.

items.activity: Eat local in the market
items.note: Boat noodles, khanom krok, old-style coffee, seasonal fruit and Thai sweets are all easy to find, both on the boats and at the canal-side stalls.

items.activity: Pick up souvenirs before leaving the market
items.note: Coconut sugar, fruit, dried goods and small pottery keepsakes — plenty to grab to take home.

items.activity: Lunch around Damnoen Saduak before the drive back
items.note: There are local restaurants and canal-side spots to choose from here. Fill up before getting in the car.

items.activity: Set off back to Bangkok
items.note: It's about 1.5 hours from Damnoen Saduak back to Bangkok via Rama 2 Road. Leaving in the afternoon helps you dodge some of the Sunday-evening traffic.

blocks.html: Damnoen Saduak is an old floating market known around the world, running as a tourist spot since 1967. Its draw is the canal-side scene of paddle boats selling goods, which still survives here in part. The trick is to go early, because from mid-morning to noon the crowds build and the vendors start packing up. If you want good photos and an easy boat ride, aim to reach the market before 8 am. As for boat fares, settle the price clearly before you get on so there's no confusion afterwards.

blocks.title: Getting the most out of the floating market
blocks.html: Ask about and agree the boat rental clearly before boarding — both the price per boat and how long the ride lasts. Some food on the boats costs a little more than usual depending on location, so if you want cheaper prices you can walk and buy along the canal bank instead. And bring plenty of cash, as many stalls still don't take transfers.

blocks.text: What else is there to do in Ratchaburi if you have more time

blocks.html: If you've still got energy on day two, or want to stretch the trip to four days, Ratchaburi has plenty more spots to drop by — nature, craft and photo-friendly stops alike. Add them in to taste.

items.name: Rueang Khong Ong
items.blurb: A living museum telling the story of Ratchaburi's dragon jars, with pottery workshops and ceramic photo corners — a natural follow-on from Tao Hong Tai.

items.name: The Scenery Vintage Farm
items.blurb: A European-style vintage sheep farm that photographs well, with a café and a spot to feed the sheep — good for families and photo lovers.

items.name: Wat Nong Hoi (Khao Wat Nong Hoi)
items.blurb: A hilltop temple where you climb up to pay respects to Guan Yin and take in views over Ratchaburi town, with cool air in the early morning and evening.

items.name: Old Mae Klong riverside market
items.blurb: A quarter of old shophouses and a riverside market in town — stroll, sample local food and photograph the street art.

blocks.text: Best eats across the two provinces: Phetchaburi–Ratchaburi

blocks.html: A cross-province trip like this gives you two styles of food: the Phetchaburi side is strong on sweets and regional dishes, while the Ratchaburi side leans into canal-side eats and local food around Damnoen Saduak. These are the dishes you can actually find and that people go for again and again, ordered to match the flow of the trip.

items.name: Phetchaburi mor kaeng custard
items.blurb: Phetchaburi's signature souvenir — a rich, fragrant custard made from egg, palm sugar and coconut milk. Famous shops line Phetkasem Road on the way into and out of town, easy to grab and take home.

items.name: Phetchaburi khao chae
items.blurb: Rice in chilled, flower-scented water eaten with fried side dishes — Phetchaburi's hot-season cooler. Most reliably found March–May, and the old-town shops do it well.
items.meta: Hot-season dish · around 80–150 THB per set

items.name: Thong yip, thong yot, foi thong
items.blurb: Traditional Thai sweets that Phetchaburi does very well, sweet and fragrant from egg and sugar. Find them in the old town and at souvenir shops all over town.

items.name: Damnoen Saduak boat noodles
items.blurb: Small bowls of rich-broth boat noodles, the classic floating-market eat — order several bowls without filling up too fast, with pork crackling and meatballs on the side.
items.meta: Canal-side savoury · from 15–20 THB per bowl

items.name: Charcoal-fired khanom krok & sweets in the floating market
items.blurb: Coconut-scented khanom krok from a charcoal stove, plus Thai sweets made fresh in Damnoen Saduak floating market — eaten warm by the canal, it suits the setting.

items.name: Old-style canal-side coffee
items.blurb: Oliang and old-style coffee brewed fresh in the floating market and old market — bold and sweet in the traditional way, sipped with pa thong ko in the morning.

items.name: Thai food at Khao Ngu view restaurants
items.blurb: Thai restaurants with limestone-hill and rice-paddy views around Khao Ngu — à la carte dishes, grilled fish and tom yum at friendly prices, good for day-two lunch.
items.meta: À la carte · around 80–250 THB per dish

items.name: Tao Hong Tai café
items.blurb: A café inside the old ceramics factory, where you sip coffee among the pottery and dragon jars — a different atmosphere from your usual café, and the factory is free to visit.

items.name: Palm sugar & coconut sugar from both provinces
items.blurb: The Phetchaburi side is known for palm sugar from toddy palms, while the Damnoen Saduak side is known for coconut sugar — both are used in sweets and make good souvenirs.

blocks.title: Pacing your eating
blocks.html: Phetchaburi sweets keep, so buy them on the way back on the last day and they'll be fresher. Floating-market food has to be eaten fresh on the spot. Carry plenty of cash, since many small stalls still don't take transfers. Fried snacks and sweets in the floating market vary in price by location, so it's fine to compare a couple of stalls before buying.

blocks.text: The route and getting between the provinces

items: Bangkok → Phetchaburi — Rama 2 Road through Samut Sakhon–Samut Songkhram, or Phetkasem Road through Nakhon Pathom–Ratchaburi, about 2 hours to the town centre.
Phetchaburi → Ratchaburi — take Phetkasem Road (Highway 4) north, through Pak Tho district, about 54 km and roughly 1 hour.
Ratchaburi → Damnoen Saduak — about 30 km, roughly 40 minutes, from Ratchaburi town. Stay near the market to do it early the next morning.
Damnoen Saduak → Bangkok — back into Bangkok via Rama 2 Road, about 1.5 hours. Leaving in the afternoon helps dodge the evening jams.

If you're not driving — vans and trains run between Phetchaburi and Ratchaburi, but renting a car or hiring one in town is recommended, since the sights are spread out beyond the towns and the floating market is hard to reach by public transport.

faq.q: Is it worth doing Phetchaburi and Ratchaburi together, and how many days do you need?
faq.a: Yes — the two provinces are next to each other, about 54 km apart, an hour's drive. Three days works best: day one for Phetchaburi's old town and Khao Wang, day two up to Ratchaburi for Tao Hong Tai and Khao Ngu, day three an early start at Damnoen Saduak floating market before heading home. If you're short on time, you can trim it to 2 days by cutting some of the Ratchaburi stops.

faq.q: What time does Damnoen Saduak floating market open, and when should you go?
faq.a: The market gets busy from early on, around 07:00, through to about midday when it starts to wind down. Aim to arrive before 8 am for the traditional paddle-boat scene, fewer crowds and better photos. By mid-morning it gets busy and the vendors start packing up.

faq.q: How do you get from Phetchaburi to Ratchaburi, and is it far?
faq.a: It's about 54 km city centre to city centre via Phetkasem Road (Highway 4), heading north through Pak Tho district, roughly 1 hour's drive. If you're not driving, vans and trains run between the two cities, but for sights spread out beyond the towns, renting a car is more flexible.

faq.q: Are Tao Hong Tai and Khao Ngu free to visit, and what are the hours?
faq.a: Tao Hong Tai is free to visit, open about 08:00–17:00, with an in-house workshop and café. Khao Ngu Stone Park is a public park you can stroll and photograph, about 8 km from town. Both pair well in one day with Ratchaburi's old town.

faq.q: Where do you stay on this trip?
faq.a: Stay in Phetchaburi town on the first night so you're set to drive up to Ratchaburi the next morning. On the second night, stay around Damnoen Saduak or near the floating market so you can be up early for the market atmosphere. If you want the beach, you can add a night in Cha-am at the end.

quickAnswerHtml: A two-province road trip through Phetchaburi and Ratchaburi, Thailand: old-town temples and Khao Wang, then Ratchaburi's Tao Hong Tai pottery and Khao Ngu, ending at Damnoen Saduak floating market — with times, prices and a route that never doubles back.
